marginaleffects methods for mvgam objects

Source: R/marginaleffects.mvgam.R
mvgam_marginaleffects.Rd

These methods let marginaleffects::predictions(), marginaleffects::slopes() and marginaleffects::comparisons() take an mvgam fit. get_predict() returns the posterior draws in the posterior_draws attribute. marginaleffects computes every summary from those draws. The uncertainty comes from the draws alone. marginaleffects also calls get_coef(), get_vcov() and set_coef(). Their output leaves every result unchanged.

Prediction scale

mvgam registers three type values with marginaleffects:

  • "expected": the expectation E[Y]. Most other model classes call this "response".

  • "response": predictive draws with observation noise, on the outcome scale. A count family gives integers.

  • "link": the linear predictor.

marginaleffects takes "response" as the default. Pass type = "expected" for the expectation. comparisons() and slopes() replace "response" with "expected". A contrast differences two predictions. Observation noise in each would widen it. A slope also divides that noise by a small step. The result keeps the label "response". predictions() on "response" keeps the observation noise. marginaleffects summarises the draws by their posterior median. For a right-skewed predictive distribution the median falls below the mean.

The latent trend

By default (process_error = FALSE) each prediction takes the covariate part of the trend: the effects in its formula, without its innovations. Each posterior draw keeps its own coefficients. The result shows the effect of the covariates with the latent process at its mean. Its credible band leaves out the uncertainty of the latent state.

Under a nonlinear link this falls short of the model's own E[Y]. Averaging over the innovations of an AR(1) trend raises a log-link expectation by the factor \(\exp(\sigma^2 / (2(1 - \rho^2)))\). process_error = TRUE adds the innovations. Slopes and comparisons then describe E[Y], with wider bands.

When the trend explains most of the variation in a series, the covariates have little left to explain under either setting. hindcast.mvgam() and forecast.mvgam() return the state the model inferred.

References

Arel-Bundock, V., Greifer, N. and Heiss, A. (2024). How to interpret statistical models using marginaleffects for R and Python. Journal of Statistical Software, 111(9):1-32. doi:10.18637/jss.v111.i09

See also

conditional_effects.mvgam() for quick effect plots, posterior_epred.mvgam() for the predictions these methods take.

Examples

# \dontrun{
library(marginaleffects)
set.seed(1)
simdat <- sim_mvgam(n_series = 1L, n_timepoints = 60L,
                    trend_model = AR())
mod <- mvgam(y ~ s(x, k = 5), trend_formula = ~ AR(p = 1),
             data = simdat$data_train, family = poisson(),
             chains = 2, silent = 2)
#> Error: 'y' has values outside the support of family 'poisson'.
#>   Requires: 0 <= 'y' (integers only).
#>   Observed range: [-2.504, 2.943]. 23 of 45 values fall outside, the first
#>   at row 1.
#>   Check the column for missing-data sentinels such as -1 or -999.

# Average change in the expected count per unit of x
avg_slopes(mod, variables = "x", type = "expected")
#> Error: object 'mod' not found

# The same slope with the trend's innovations averaged in
avg_slopes(mod, variables = "x", type = "expected",
           process_error = TRUE)
#> Error: object 'mod' not found

# Expected counts across the range of x
plot_predictions(mod, condition = "x", type = "expected")
#> Error: object 'mod' not found
# }
